prompt.context: It is early October, and Jimmy Smith, an MBA2 at NYU Stern, has a decision to make. After a summer interning at Firm A, Jimmy received an offer to return full-time next year. However, Jimmy also decided to re-recruit and received a competing offer from Firm B. Jimmy now needs to decide which offer he should accept, and has looked to you, his best friend, for help.
prompt.question: Which offer should Jimmy accept? Help him decide between Firm A and Firm B.

clarifying_info.q: What does Jimmy care about — money, prestige, work-life balance?
clarifying_info.a: Jimmy only cares about money and is seeking to maximize financial value.

clarifying_info.q: Is Jimmy considering any other offers or opportunities?
clarifying_info.a: No, Jimmy is not considering any other opportunities.

clarifying_info.q: How long does Jimmy plan to stay at the firm?
clarifying_info.a: Jimmy intends to work at either firm for 3 years.

clarifying_info.q: Are Firm A and Firm B in the same industry?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, they are competitors in the same industry.

clarifying_info.q: Is there a difference in prestige between the two firms?
clarifying_info.a: Firm A is considered second-tier but increasingly competes with top-tier firms for talent. Firm B is more prestigious and considered top-tier in its industry.

exhibits.title: Compensation Package by Firm
exhibits.shows: A table comparing the compensation components of Firm A and Firm B, including starting salary, signing bonus, expected annual bonus, and tuition reimbursement with footnotes on timing.

exhibits.title: Salary Growth by Firm
exhibits.shows: A chart showing projected annual salary growth over 3 years for Firm A and Firm B. Note states annual bonus is expected to remain constant.

data.note: Annual bonus expected to remain constant

exhibits.title: Distribution of Expected Starting Salaries for Exit Opportunities
exhibits.shows: A bar chart showing the probability distribution of expected starting salaries ($150k–$250k) for exit opportunities from Top-Tier vs. Second-Tier firms. A note states salary will grow at 5% per year indefinitely.

data.note: Assume salary will grow at 5% per year indefinitely

framework: Identify all sources of compensation: base salary, signing bonus, annual bonus, tuition reimbursement
Apply time value of money — discount all cash flows to present value (DCF/NPV framework)
Brainstorm non-financial and long-term financial factors (exit opportunities, firm culture, training, travel)
Quantify the value of exit opportunities by computing expected value of year-4 salary at each firm
Determine whether exit opportunity differential flips the 3-year NPV conclusion

questions.prompt: Calculate the NPV of each firm's 3-year compensation package and determine which offer is financially superior over 3 years.
questions.guidance: Candidate must lay out year-by-year cash flows for both firms (Year 0 = signing bonus; Years 1–3 = salary + annual bonus, plus tuition reimbursement for Firm A at Year 3). Candidate should apply a simplified discount: divide by (1+r)^n. The casebook uses a ~10% discount rate simplified to round numbers (Year 1 ÷ 1.1 ≈ round, Year 2 ÷ 1.21 ≈ round, Year 3 ÷ 1.33 ≈ round). After discounting, Firm A NPV = $440k vs Firm B NPV = $430k — Firm A wins the 3-year comparison by ~$10k.

math.setup: List undiscounted cash flows, then apply PV = CF / (1+r)^n with r ≈ 10% (simplified to round numbers). Year 0 is undiscounted.
steps: Firm A undiscounted totals — Year 0: $30k (signing); Year 1: $91k salary + $30k bonus = $121k; Year 2: $114k + $30k = $144k; Year 3: $126k + $30k + $78k tuition = $234k
Firm B undiscounted totals — Year 0: $40k (signing); Year 1: $97k + $35k = $132k; Year 2: $121k + $35k = $156k; Year 3: $147k + $35k = $182k
Simplified DCF (round numbers used in casebook) — Firm A: $30 + $110 + $120 + $180 = $440k; Firm B: $40 + $120 + $130 + $140 = $430k
Firm A NPV ≈ $440k; Firm B NPV ≈ $430k → Firm A leads by ~$10k over 3 years
math.answer: Firm A has a higher 3-year NPV of approximately $440k vs. Firm B's $430k — a $10k advantage for Firm A.

questions.prompt: After the brainstorm, focus on exit opportunities. Using Exhibit 3, calculate the expected value of year-4 starting salary at each firm and determine whether this changes the recommendation.
questions.guidance: Step 1 — compute expected value (probability-weighted salary) for each firm. Firm A expected value = $185k; Firm B expected value = $220k (difference = $35k). Alternatively candidate may use the median (Firm A ≈ $175k, Firm B ≈ $225k, difference = $50k) if they justify the choice. Step 2 — discount the year-4 salary differential to present value using PV = FV / (1+r)^4, simplified as FV / 1.4. PV of $35k differential ≈ $25k; PV of $50k median differential ≈ $35.7k. Either way, the PV of the exit-opportunity advantage ($25k–$36k) exceeds the $10k 3-year NPV lead of Firm A, flipping the recommendation to Firm B. Note: the 5% salary growth rate is a red herring — it only widens the disparity and does not change the outcome.

math.setup: Expected Value (EV) = sum of (Salary × Probability) for each salary band. Then PV = EV_differential / (1 + r)^4 with r ≈ 10%, simplified as / 1.4.
steps: Difference in expected year-4 salary: $220k − $185k = $35k (mean method)
PV of $35k differential discounted 4 years at 10% (simplified): $35k / 1.4 ≈ $25k
Since $25k PV of exit-opportunity advantage > $10k Firm A 3-year NPV lead, Firm B is the better choice
math.answer: PV of exit-opportunity salary differential ≈ $25k (mean) to $35.7k (median), which exceeds the $10k 3-year advantage of Firm A. Firm B is the financially superior choice.

brainstorming.prompt: What other things should Jimmy consider before making a decision? Beyond the financial calculations, what factors — both financial and non-financial — should Jimmy weigh as his friend and advisor?

categories.name: Financial
ideas: Exit opportunities and long-term earning potential
Firm financial stability and risk of layoffs
Potential for above-average raises or promotions at each firm
Value of equity or partnership track (if applicable)

categories.name: Non-Financial
ideas: Focus and type of work at each firm (deal flow, client mix, sector focus)
Geographic location and commute / travel requirements
Training quality and professional development programs
Firm's reputation effect on resume / brand value for future roles
Cultural fit and personal happiness / work-life balance

recommendation: Jimmy should accept the offer from Firm B.

Although Firm A offers a slightly higher 3-year NPV (~$440k vs. ~$430k), the expected value of exit opportunities from Firm B (a top-tier firm) more than compensates for this $10k difference. The present value of the exit-salary advantage is approximately $25k–$36k, making Firm B the superior long-term financial choice.
risks: Firm B encounters financial challenges and lays off staff before Jimmy completes 3 years.
Jimmy underperforms at the more demanding Firm B and does not realize the better exit opportunities.
Firm B is a poor cultural fit, causing Jimmy to leave early and forfeiting the financial upside.
next_steps: Leverage the Firm A offer to negotiate a better compensation package at Firm B (salary, signing bonus).
Conduct further due diligence on each firm — attend sell days, speak with current employees, assess cultural fit and type of work.
Hold off on signing until the last possible moment to gather maximum information from both firms' sell days.
